narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 56.8% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The three factors that mattered most in this decision were, in order: your LSAT score, your class ranking after the third year of law school, and your undergraduate GPA. Your LSAT score was the strongest influence and it pushed the prediction toward passing. However, the other two features pulled strongly in the opposite direction and ultimately outweighed that positive signal.

Your third-year class ranking placed you in the second decile, well below the average of roughly sixth decile among students who were accepted. This low standing signaled to the model a higher risk of struggling with the bar exam. Similarly, your undergraduate GPA of 2.5 is noticeably lower than the 3.23 average of accepted applicants, which further increased the predicted chance of failure. Your family income and plan to attend full-time were considered but had far less impact on the outcome.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your class rank in the remaining law school years and consider retaking the LSAT if possible. Strengthening these academic signals will give future applications a much better chance of success. (218 words)
